tagline.text: A white-sand cove over 1 km long in Santa Ana, northern Cagayan, reached by boat

location.label: Location
location.text: Barangay San Vicente, Santa Ana, Cagayan

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: March–May dry season, on calm-wave days

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,500–4,000 (estimate including boat, entrance, and meals; transport excluded)

children.text: Anguib Beach is a white-sand cove more than 1 km long in the San Vicente area of Santa Ana at the northern end of Cagayan. Many sources put the boat ride from San Vicente Port at about 25 minutes, but the sources are dated, so check fees locally.

Anguib Beach lies in Barangay San Vicente, Santa Ana, Cagayan, near the northeastern tip of Luzon. Fine white sand runs for more than a kilometer, tall trees line the shore, and green hills rise behind. In the sheltered cove the water is said to shift from sky blue to deep blue on calm days. One travel blogger wrote that the sand was whiter, the water clearer, and the waves calmer than at Saud Beach in Pagudpud, Ilocos Norte. For this reason the beach earned the nickname "Boracay of the North." These assessments rest on reviews from 2012–2019, so check what it looks like now when you get there.

Most sources say the boat ride from San Vicente Port takes about 25 minutes, but one blogger said it took close to an hour because of rough waves. You can also reach it overland by tricycle or by driving, though one review says you must walk several meters to the beach. There are no shops at the beach, so bring food and drink, and since Santa Ana has no ATM you need to carry cash. An old review says the caretakers can arrange a fresh seafood meal. Facilities are simple: there are cottages and toilet and shower areas, and you can camp overnight in a tent, but most sources say there is no proper resort.

Boat fees differ by source. A 2022 blog and a guide updated in July 2026 list ₱1,500–1,800 per boat (up to 8 people, plus ₱500 for an overnight stay) round trip from San Vicente Port to Anguib Beach alone, while the ₱3,500 island-hopping price to Anguib, Cape Engaño, and Crocodile Island comes only from a 2012 guide and has not been confirmed recently. Entrance was ₱50 in 2012 and ₱100 in 2013–2014; the 2026 guide says ₱100 by day and ₱150 overnight, and the 2022 blog lists ₱50 for Santa Ana residents and ₱100 for outsiders plus a ₱20 environmental fee, while the 2026 guide separately lists a ₱50–70 environmental fee around Palaui, a ₱20 trash fee, and a refundable ₱200 deposit. Prices change from year to year, so check current fees at the Santa Ana tourism office. A 2019 article says the beach is being developed by the Cagayan Economic Zone Authority (CEZA) together with the Santa Ana local government.

Nearby are Cape Engaño Lighthouse and Punta Verde on Palaui Island. Combining Anguib with a Palaui Island trip is efficient, but reviews mention separate charges for a lighthouse guide (about ₱300) and a snorkeling guide on the Palaui side, so the costs overlap. Advice is to include the beach as one stop on an island-hopping day and return before the afternoon waves get rough. At San Vicente Port you register at the visitor center and pay the fees, then hire a boat from the accredited boatmen's cooperative. Boats are rented per boat, with fees set by destination and time, so going with a group cuts the cost per person considerably. Guidance for Palaui also describes a trash deposit that is returned after your trash is checked on your return, so carrying all your trash back from the beach is the rule. Whether boats go out when the sea is rough is decided at the port on the morning itself, so leave some slack in your plans. Palaui Island across from Anguib was declared a marine reserve in 1994, and in 2018 a law upgraded about 80 km² including the surrounding sea to a protected landscape and seascape, so development in this area is strictly limited. For that reason, do not step on or touch the coral and leave no trash or single-use items behind. Electricity and signal are limited at both places, so bring a power bank and keep your phone in a waterproof pouch.

blocks.title: A White-Sand Cove Over 1 km Long

children.text: Fine white sand runs along the cove, and trees along the shore provide shade. It is described as quiet, with few people.
Inside the cove the water is calm on many days, which suits swimming, sunbathing, and light activities such as kayaking or boat rides. Some stretches are shallow and rocky, so check your footing.
According to reviews, the area with the best view charges a higher fee, while a shallow, rocky area a few meters away is cheaper. Confirm the exact areas and fees on site.
A boat circuit through Anguib Beach, Cape Engaño, and Crocodile Island is described. It pairs well with the lighthouse and Punta Verde on Palaui Island for a full day.
The San Vicente area is described as having a mangrove forest and Crocodile Island, named for its crocodile-like shape. Ask at the port whether it can be added to your boat trip.
Cottages and tent camping are described as possible. An old review says a tent cost ₱400 in 2012, which may differ now. Confirm camping rules locally.

blocks.title: Remote Calm at the End of Northern Luzon

children.text: It is a remote spot 3–4 hours overland from Tuguegarao, and many reviews describe few visitors and a quiet atmosphere. If you dislike crowded beaches, the difficult access works in its favor.

25 minutes to 1 hour
You can also use a tricycle or vehicle overland to near the beach, but reviews say you walk the last stretch.

Calm waves matter most for a beach trip. The dry months of March–May are generally the most stable, but this area is affected by the northeast monsoon and the sea can be rough in winter. Check sea conditions at the port before heading out.
Mornings are best. Reviews say waves get rougher in the afternoon, so plan to return around midday.

Accommodation and boats can fill up early during the March–May peak and on holidays, so contact them in advance. Weekday mornings, on the other hand, are described as quiet. In typhoon season the port is sometimes closed, so check sea-condition notices before you go.

There is no proper resort at the beach, only cottages and tents. The usual plan is to stay in Santa Ana town or Tuguegarao and make it a day trip.

There are no shops at the beach, so prepare water, food, and snacks in town. Reviews say the caretakers can arrange a seafood meal, so ask at the port. Santa Ana has no ATM, so withdraw cash in Tuguegarao beforehand.

Santa Ana is a small town with few places to stay and eat. To catch an early boat it is easiest to stay the night before in Santa Ana town, and in peak season and on holidays lodging and boats can fill early, so contact them in advance. Many visitors pack a lunch from the town market or shops.

Santa Ana is a small town and reportedly has no ATM, so withdraw cash in Tuguegarao beforehand and bring a simple snack if you arrive late. Set a departure time from the beach in case the weather turns suddenly.
